title: Chapter 60 — The Line
paragraphs: With reference to the whaling scene soon to be described, as well as for the better understanding of all similar scenes presented elsewhere, I must speak here of the magical, sometimes horrible whale-line.

The line originally used in the fishery was of the best hemp, only lightly treated with tar vapor, not saturated with tar as ordinary ropes are. For while tar, as ordinarily used, makes the hemp more pliable for the ropemaker, and also makes the rope itself more convenient for the sailor in common ship use, not only would the ordinary quantity stiffen the whale-line too much for the close coiling it must undergo; but, as most seamen are beginning to learn, tar in general by no means adds to a rope's durability or strength, however much compactness and gloss it may give it.

In recent years, Manila rope has in the American fishery almost entirely replaced hemp as a material for whale-lines. Though not as durable as hemp, it is stronger and far more soft and elastic. And I will add — since there is an aesthetics in all things — it is much more handsome and becoming to the boat than hemp. Hemp is a dusky, dark fellow, a sort of Indian; but Manila is like a golden-haired Circassian to look at.

The whale-line is only two-thirds of an inch thick. At first sight you would not think it as strong as it really is. By experiment, each of its fifty-one yarns will suspend a weight of one hundred and twenty pounds, so that the whole rope will bear a strain nearly equal to three tons. In length, the common sperm whale-line measures something over two hundred fathoms. Toward the stern of the boat it is spirally coiled away in the tub — not like the worm-pipe (the coiled tube) of a still, though, but so as to form one round, cheese-shaped mass of densely bedded "sheaves," or layers of concentric spirals, without any hollow except the "heart," the tiny vertical tube formed at the axis of the cheese. Since the least tangle or kink in the coiling would, as the line ran out, infallibly take off somebody's arm, leg, or entire body, the utmost care is taken in stowing the line in its tub. Some harpooners will spend almost an entire morning at this business, carrying the line high aloft and then reeving it downward through a block toward the tub, so as to free it of every possible wrinkle and twist in the act of coiling.

In the English boats two tubs are used instead of one, the same line being continuously coiled in both tubs. There is some advantage in this, because these twin tubs, being so small, fit more readily into the boat and do not strain it so much; whereas the American tub, nearly three feet in diameter and of proportionate depth, makes rather bulky freight for a craft whose planks are only half an inch thick; for the bottom of the whale-boat is like ice at the critical point, which will bear up a considerable weight if it is spread out, but not very much if it is concentrated. When the painted canvas cover is clapped on the American line-tub, the boat looks as if it were pulling off with a prodigious great wedding-cake to present to the whales.

Both ends of the line are exposed; the lower end finishes in an eye-splice, or loop, which comes up from the bottom against the side of the tub and hangs over its edge, completely free of everything. This arrangement of the lower end is necessary for two reasons. First: to make it easier to fasten to it an additional line from a neighboring boat, in case the struck whale should sound (dive) so deep as to threaten to carry off the entire line originally attached to the harpoon. In these instances the whale is, of course, passed like a mug of ale, as it were, from the one boat to the other; though the first boat always hovers close by to assist its partner. Second: this arrangement is indispensable for common safety's sake; for if the lower end of the line were in any way attached to the boat, and the whale were then to run the line out to the end almost in a single smoking minute, as he sometimes does, he would not stop there, for the doomed boat would infallibly be dragged down after him into the depths of the sea; and in that case no town-crier would ever find her again.

Before the boat is lowered for the chase, the upper end of the line is brought aft from the tub, taken around the loggerhead there (a stout wooden post in the stern), and then carried forward again along the whole length of the boat. It rests crosswise on the loom, or handle, of every man's oar, so that it bumps against his wrist as he rows, and it also runs between the men, who sit alternately at opposite gunwales, up to the leaded chocks, or grooves, in the sharp tip of the prow, where a wooden pin or skewer about the size of an ordinary quill keeps it from slipping out. From the chocks it hangs in a slight festoon over the bows and then comes back inside the boat. Some ten or twenty fathoms of it (called box-line) are coiled on the box in the bows, and from there it goes on to the gunwale a little farther aft, where it is fastened to the short-warp — the rope attached directly to the harpoon. Before that connection is made, though, the short-warp goes through various mystifications too tedious to describe.

Thus the whale-line folds the whole boat in its complicated coils, twisting and writhing around it in almost every direction. All the oarsmen are caught up in its perilous contortions, so that to the timid eye of the landsman they seem like Indian jugglers, with the deadliest snakes playfully draped around their limbs. No son of mortal woman can seat himself for the first time amid those hempen intricacies and, while straining his utmost at the oar, reflect that at any unknown instant the harpoon may be darted and all these horrible contortions be set in play like ringed lightning — no one can be placed like that without a shudder that makes the very marrow in his bones quiver like a shaken jelly. Yet habit — strange thing! what can habit not accomplish? — livelier sallies, merrier mirth, better jokes, and brighter repartee you never heard over your mahogany dinner table than you will hear over the half-inch white cedar of the whale-boat, when it is hung with hangman's nooses like this; and, like the six burghers of Calais before King Edward, the six men who make up the crew pull into the jaws of death with a halter around every neck, as you might say.

Perhaps a very little thought will now enable you to account for those repeated whaling disasters — some few of which are casually recorded — of this man or that man being taken out of the boat by the line and lost. For when the line is darting out, to be seated in the boat then is like being seated in the midst of the manifold whizzings of a steam-engine in full play, when every flying beam and shaft and wheel is grazing you. It is worse; for you cannot sit motionless in the heart of these perils, because the boat is rocking like a cradle, and you are pitched one way and the other without the slightest warning; and only by a certain self-adjusting buoyancy, and by willing and acting in the same instant, can you escape being made a Mazeppa of (like Byron's hero, lashed to a runaway horse) and carried off where the all-seeing sun himself could never pick you out.

Again: the deep calm that only seems to come before the storm and foretell it is perhaps more dreadful than the storm itself, since the calm is really just the wrapper and envelope of the storm, holding it inside, as the harmless-looking rifle holds the deadly powder, the ball, and the explosion. In the same way, the graceful repose of the line as it silently snakes around the oarsmen before it comes into actual play carries more real terror than any other part of this dangerous business. But why say more? All men live wrapped in whale-lines. All are born with nooses around their necks; but mortals only realize the silent, subtle, ever-present dangers of life when they are caught in the swift, sudden turn of death. And if you are a philosopher, then sitting in the whale-boat you would not feel one bit more terror at heart than if you were sitting by your evening fire with a poker, not a harpoon, beside you.
